final_note: You worked through Properties of electromagnetic waves 2 — 8 specification statements.

concepts.def: A repeated back-and-forth change of the current in a circuit, so that the charges move first one way and then the other, over and over. (HT only) Oscillations of this kind in an electrical circuit can produce radio waves.
(HT only) Radio waves can be produced by oscillations in electrical circuits. The oscillating circuit is the source: the faster the oscillation, the higher the frequency of the radio wave produced.

(HT only) When radio waves are absorbed they may create an alternating current, so radio waves can themselves induce oscillations in an electrical circuit. Production and absorption are therefore two directions of the same link between radio waves and oscillating circuits.

concepts.term: Frequency of the induced alternating current
concepts.def: (HT only) The alternating current created when a radio wave is absorbed has the same frequency as the radio wave itself. A 200 kHz radio wave absorbed by a circuit induces an alternating current of 200 kHz.

concepts.term: Atoms and nuclei as sources of electromagnetic waves
concepts.def: Changes in atoms and the nuclei of atoms can result in electromagnetic waves being generated or absorbed over a wide frequency range. The same atom can therefore be involved in emitting or absorbing radiation from very different parts of the electromagnetic spectrum.
Gamma rays originate from changes in the nucleus of an atom. This origin, rather than any figure for frequency or wavelength, is what the specification uses to identify where gamma rays come from.

Radiation dose is a measure of the risk of harm resulting from an exposure of the body to radiation. It is not a count of the radiation itself: it combines how much radiation the body received with how damaging that type of radiation is.
The sievert is the unit in which radiation dose is measured. A dose quoted in sieverts tells you about the risk of harm from an exposure, so a larger number of sieverts means a greater risk of harm.

A smaller unit of radiation dose, used for the everyday doses people actually receive. 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv), so to convert a dose in mSv to Sv you divide by 1000, and to convert Sv to mSv you multiply by 1000.
X-rays and gamma rays are ionising radiation. Being ionising is what makes them hazardous to human body tissue: they can cause the mutation of genes and cancer.
Ultraviolet waves can have hazardous effects on human body tissue: they can cause skin to age prematurely and increase the risk of skin cancer.
A change to a gene caused by ionising radiation. X-rays and gamma rays are ionising radiation that can cause the mutation of genes and cancer.

Using data you are given about radiation doses to compare exposures and comment on the risks and consequences. Doing this properly means converting all the doses to the same unit before comparing them, and stating conclusions as differences in risk rather than as certain outcomes.

mcqs.q: How can radio waves be produced?
options: By oscillations in an electrical circuit
By changes in the nucleus of an atom
By changes in the electrons of an atom
By heating a metal until it glows brightly
mcqs.explain: This is exactly what the specification states: radio waves can be produced by oscillations in electrical circuits.

mcqs.q: Which statement best describes what happens when a radio wave is absorbed by an electrical circuit?
options: It heats the circuit but produces no current at all
It creates a direct current in one fixed direction
It induces oscillations, creating an alternating current
It creates a current whose frequency the circuit sets
mcqs.explain: When radio waves are absorbed they may create an alternating current, so radio waves can themselves induce oscillations in an electrical circuit.

mcqs.q: A transmitter circuit oscillates at 200 kHz and emits a radio wave. A distant circuit absorbs that wave. What alternating current is induced in the distant circuit?
options: 400 kHz, twice that of the radio wave
200 kHz, the same as the radio wave
0 Hz, since a direct current is induced
100 kHz, half that of the radio wave
mcqs.explain: The alternating current created has the same frequency as the radio wave itself, so the 200 kHz wave induces a 200 kHz current.

options: In changes in the nucleus of an atom
In the vibration of the whole atom
In oscillations in an electrical circuit
In changes in the electrons of an atom
mcqs.explain: The specification states that gamma rays originate from changes in the nucleus of an atom.

mcqs.q: A student writes: 'X-rays must come from the nucleus, because they are ionising like gamma rays.' What is wrong with this?
options: Nothing is wrong; all ionising radiation is nuclear
Only gamma rays are stated to come from the nucleus
Gamma rays come from the electrons, not the nucleus
Gamma rays are not ionising, so the comparison fails
mcqs.explain: X-rays and gamma rays are named together as ionising radiation, but only gamma rays are attributed to changes in the nucleus of an atom.

mcqs.q: What does a radiation dose, given in sieverts, measure?
options: The risk of harm from an exposure to radiation
The frequency of the radiation absorbed
The number of gamma rays that reach the body
The type of radiation the body is exposed to
mcqs.explain: Radiation dose is a measure of the risk of harm resulting from an exposure of the body to the radiation.

mcqs.q: Two people are exposed to the same type of radiation, but one receives four times the dose of the other. What conclusion can be drawn?
options: The risk depends only on how long each exposure was
The greater dose carries the greater risk of harm
The risk is the same, as the type of radiation is the same
The greater dose is certain to cause that person cancer
mcqs.explain: The effects depend on the type of radiation and the size of the dose, and dose measures the risk of harm, so the larger dose means the larger risk.

mcqs.q: A worker receives a radiation dose of 2500 mSv. What is this dose in sieverts (Sv)?
options: 2.5 Sv
mcqs.explain: 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv), so 2500 mSv is divided by 1000 to give 2.5 Sv.

mcqs.q: A table gives these average doses: chest X-ray 0.02 mSv; CT scan of the abdomen 8 mSv; natural background radiation 2.7 mSv per year. Which conclusion is valid?
options: One chest X-ray gives a larger dose than one CT scan
A CT scan is certain to cause that patient to get cancer
Background radiation is harmless because it is natural
One CT scan gives about three years' worth of background
mcqs.explain: 8 mSv divided by 2.7 mSv per year is about 3 years, and all three figures are already in the same unit, so the comparison is valid.

mcqs.q: Worker A receives a dose of 800 mSv in a year. Worker B receives 1.2 Sv in the same year. Who receives the larger dose?
options: Neither, because the two doses are equal once converted
A, because 800 is a much bigger number than 1.2 is
B, because 1.2 Sv is 1200 mSv, more than A's 800 mSv
A, because a millisievert is larger than a sievert is
mcqs.explain: Using 1000 mSv = 1 Sv, B's dose is 1200 mSv, which is greater than A's 800 mSv, so B has the greater risk of harm.

mcqs.q: Which hazardous effect on the human body is caused by ultraviolet waves?
options: Immediate burning of tissue deep inside the body
Heating of the whole body from the inside outwards
Mutation of genes caused by ionisation of tissue
Premature ageing of the skin and skin cancer risk
mcqs.explain: Ultraviolet waves can cause skin to age prematurely and increase the risk of skin cancer.

mcqs.q: Why are X-rays and gamma rays described as hazardous to human body tissue?
options: They heat body tissue very quickly, causing severe burns
They age the skin, but do not reach the deeper tissue
They are ionising and can cause gene mutation and cancer
They travel at very high speed right through the body
mcqs.explain: X-rays and gamma rays are ionising radiation that can cause the mutation of genes and cancer.
